d.e: Near-synonyms: break apart, break up, take apart, tear down, tear up

d.t: (ergative, figuratively) To divide into parts to give more details, to provide a more indepth analysis of.
d.e: Near-synonym: analyze

d.t: (ergative) To digest.
d.e: Near-synonym: catabolize

d.t: (informal, music) To bust down or bust a move; to perform energetic, often freestyle or hip-hop moves, frequently during a song’s instrumental break where only drums or bass are playing; see breakdown.
Alternative form of breakdown.
(transitive, idiomatic) To enter illegally or by force, especially in order to commit a crime.
d.e: Somebody broke into his car and stole his tools and CDs.

d.t: (transitive, idiomatic) To open or begin to use.
d.e: I finally broke into the second package of cookies.

d.t: (transitive, idiomatic) To successfully enter a profession or business.
d.e: He hopes to break into show business.

d.t: (transitive) To begin suddenly.
d.e: The horse broke into a gallop as they neared the barn.

d.t: (transitive, ditransitive) To transport toward somebody/somewhere.
d.e: Waiter, please bring me a single malt whiskey.

d.t: (transitive, figuratively) To supply or contribute.
d.e: The new company director brought a fresh perspective on sales and marketing.

d.t: (transitive) To occasion or bring about.
d.e: Let's bring our differences to an issue.

d.t: (transitive) To raise (a lawsuit, charges, etc.) against somebody.
To persuade; to induce; to draw; to lead; to guide.
To produce in exchange; to sell for; to fetch.
d.e: What does coal bring per ton?

d.t: (baseball) To pitch, often referring to a particularly hard thrown fastball.
d.e: The closer Jones can really bring it.

d.t: (chess) To move a piece into a more active position, esp. to initially develop it.
d.e: You want to bring the rook and then start pushing your pawns.

d.t: The sound of a telephone ringing.
d.e: Near-synonyms: ring-a-ding, ding-a-ling

d.t: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see bring, up: To bring from a lower to a higher position.
d.e: When you're in the basement, can you bring up the paints?

d.t: To mention.
d.e: Don't bring up politics if you want to have a quiet conversation with that guy.

d.t: To raise or rear (children).
d.e: She did well enough bringing up two sons and a daughter on her own.

d.t: To uncover, to bring from obscurity; to resurface (e.g. a memory)
d.e: A short Internet search brought up some amazing details of this story.

d.t: To turn on power or start, as of a machine.
d.e: Wait a minute while I bring up my computer.

d.t: (electronics) To check (a newly-assembled printed circuit board) for errors.
d.e: Anyone who's been tasked with bringing up a board knows how trying it is.

d.t: To vomit.
d.e: I was very ill today; I kept bringing up everything I ate.

d.t: To stop or interrupt a flow or steady motion.
(cricket) To reach a particular score, especially a milestone.
d.e: Warner smacked a four over midwicket to bring up his century.

d.t: To legally charge and put on trial; to position (someone) for judgement or examination by authority.
(obsolete, printing) To level type or make it ready for printing by overlaying it.
(transitive) To prepare a vein for an injection.
Son of the same parents as another person.
A male having at least one parent in common with another person (see half-brother, stepbrother).
A male fellow member of a religious community, church, trades union etc.
d.e: You shall not charge interest to your brother—interest on money or food or anything that is lent out at interest.

d.t: (informal) A form of address to a man.
d.e: Brother, can you spare a dime?

d.t: (African-American Vernacular) A fellow black man.
Somebody, usually male, connected by a common cause, situation, or affection.
Someone who is a peer, whether male or female.
(poetic) Someone who is a kinsman or shares the same patriarch.
(transitive) To treat as a brother.
Expressing exasperation.
d.e: We're being forced to work overtime? Oh, brother!

d.t: (transitive) To form (something) by combining materials or parts.
d.e: I built a shed in my backyard.

d.t: (transitive) To develop or give form to (something) according to a plan or process.
d.e: He will build an organization equipped for success.

d.t: (transitive) To increase or strengthen (something) by adding gradually to it.
d.e: We need to build an income stream over time.

d.t: (transitive) To establish a basis for (something).
(intransitive) To form by combining materials or parts.
(intransitive) To develop in magnitude or extent.
d.e: The tension built between the sparring sisters.

d.t: (transitive, computing) To construct (software) by compiling its source code.
(intransitive, computing, of source code) To be converted into software by compilation, usually with minimal human intervention.
d.e: This code won’t build any more. Have you made any changes?

d.t: (countable, uncountable) The physique of a human or animal body, or other object; constitution or structure.
d.e: Rugby players are of sturdy build.

d.t: (computing, countable) Any of various versions of a software product as it is being developed for release to users.
d.e: The computer company has introduced a new prototype build to beta testers.

d.t: (countable) The process or period of constructing a physical object.
d.e: This new Lego set was a very nice build.

d.t: (gaming, slang, countable) A structure, such as a building, statue, pool or forest created by the player.
d.e: I made a build that looked like the Parthenon in that game.

d.t: (gaming, slang, countable) A configuration of a character's items or skills created by the player.
d.e: I made a build centered around attack speed.

d.t: (uncountable) The act or process by which something is built; construction.
d.e: The building of the bridge will be completed in a couple of weeks.

d.t: (countable) A closed structure with walls and a roof.
d.e: My sister lives in that apartment building.

d.t: (mathematics) Synonym of Tits building.
present participle and gerund of build
(countable) A specific commercial enterprise or establishment.
d.e: I left my father's business.

d.t: (countable) A person's occupation, work, or trade.
d.e: He is in the motor and insurance businesses.

d.t: (uncountable) Commercial, industrial, or professional activity.
d.e: He's such a poor cook, I can't believe he's still in business!

d.t: (uncountable) The volume or amount of commercial trade.
d.e: Business has been slow lately.

d.t: (uncountable) One's dealings; patronage.
d.e: I shall take my business elsewhere.

d.t: (uncountable) Private commercial interests taken collectively.
d.e: This proposal will satisfy both business and labor.

d.t: (uncountable) The management of commercial enterprises, or the study of such management.
d.e: I studied business at Harvard.

d.t: (countable) A particular situation or activity.
d.e: This UFO stuff is a mighty strange business.

d.t: (countable) Any activity or objective needing to be dealt with; especially, one of a financial or legal matter.
d.e: Our principal business here is to get drunk.

d.t: (uncountable) Something involving one personally.
d.e: That's none of your business.

d.t: (uncountable, parliamentary procedure) Matters that come before a body for deliberation or action.
d.e: If that concludes the announcements, we'll move on to new business.

d.t: (travel, uncountable) Business class, the class of seating provided by airlines between first class and coach.
Of, to, pertaining to, or used for purposes of conducting trade, commerce, governance, advocacy or other professional purposes.
d.e: Please do not use this phone for personal calls; it is a business phone.

d.t: Professional, businesslike, having concern for good business practice.
Supporting business, conducive to the conduct of business.
Crowded with business or activities; having a great deal going on.
d.e: Be careful crossing that busy street.

d.t: Engaged with or preoccupied by an activity or person.
d.e: The director cannot see you now: he's busy.

d.t: Having much work to do; having much to get done.
d.e: Near-synonym: swamped

d.t: Having a lot going on; complicated or intricate.
d.e: Flowers, stripes, and checks in the same fabric make for a busy pattern.

d.t: Officious; meddling.
(slang, UK, Liverpool, derogatory) A police officer.
(transitive, usually reflexive) To make somebody busy or active; to occupy.
d.e: On my vacation I'll busy myself with gardening.

d.t: Apart from, except (for), excluding.
d.e: Everyone but Father left early.

d.t: (obsolete outside Scotland) Outside of.
d.e: Away but the hoose and tell me whae's there.

d.t: (chiefly literary or poetic) Merely, only, just, no more than.
d.e: Christmas comes but once a year, so we can but wait till then.

d.t: (Australia, Geordie, Scotland, conjunctive) Though, however.
d.e: I'll have to go home early but.

d.t: Used to repeat an adverb for emphasis; simply; just; absolutely.
d.e: I would never, but never do such a thing!

d.t: However, although, nevertheless, on the other hand (introducing a clause contrary to prior belief or in contrast with the preceding clause or sentence).
d.e: She is very old but still attractive.

d.t: On the contrary, rather (as a regular adversative conjunction, introducing a word or clause in contrast or contradiction with the preceding negative clause or sentence).
d.e: I am not rich but [I am] poor.  Not John but Peter went there.

d.t: (colloquial) Used at the beginning of a sentence to express opposition to a remark.
d.e: But I never said you could do that!

d.t: Except that (introducing a subordinate clause which qualifies a negative statement); also, (archaic) with omission of the subject of the subordinate clause, acting as a negative relative, "except one that", "except such that".
d.e: I cannot but feel offended.

d.t: (colloquial) Used to link an interjection to the following remark as an intensifier.
d.e: Wow! But that's amazing!

d.t: (archaic) Without it also being the case that; unless that (introducing a necessary concomitant).
d.e: It never rains but it pours

d.t: (obsolete) Except with; unless with; without.
(obsolete) Only; solely; merely.
(obsolete) Until.
(obsolete, following a negated expression of improbability) That.
An instance of using the word "but"; an objection or caveat.
d.e: It has to be done—no ifs, ands, or buts.

d.t: (Scotland) The outer room of a small two-room cottage.
A limit; a boundary.
The end; especially the larger or thicker end, or the blunt, in distinction from the sharp, end; the butt.
(archaic or rare and humorous) Use the word "but".
d.e: But me no buts.

d.t: (transitive, ditransitive) To obtain (something) in exchange for money or goods.
d.e: Who'd Father buy the car for? He bought it for me, not for you.

d.t: (transitive, ditransitive) To obtain, especially by some sacrifice.
d.e: I've bought material comfort by foregoing my dreams.

d.t: (transitive, archaic) To suffer consequences for (something) through being deprived of something; to pay for (something one has done).
(transitive) To bribe.
d.e: He tried to buy me with gifts, but I wouldn't give up my beliefs.

d.t: (transitive) To be equivalent to in value.
d.e: The dollar doesn't buy as much as it used to.

d.t: (transitive, informal) to accept as true; to believe
d.e: I'm not going to buy your stupid excuses anymore!

d.t: (intransitive) To make a purchase or purchases, to treat (for a drink, meal or gift)
d.e: She buys for Federated.

d.t: (poker slang, transitive) To make a bluff, usually a large one.
d.e: Smith tried to buy the pot on the river with a huge bluff.

d.t: Something which is bought; a purchase.
d.e: At only $30, the second-hand kitchen table was a great buy.

d.t: Near or next to.
d.e: The mailbox is by the bus stop.

d.t: From one side of something to the other, passing close by; past.
d.e: The stream runs by our back door.

d.t: Not later than (the given time); not later than the end of (the given time interval); before.
d.e: Be back by ten o'clock!

d.t: After a given amount of time has elapsed or a given event has occurred.
d.e: By February, we were all sick of the cold.

d.t: Indicates the person or thing that does or causes something: Through the action or presence of.
Indicates the creator of a work: Existing through the authorship etc. of.
d.e: There are many well-known plays by William Shakespeare

d.t: Indicates a means of achieving something: Involving/using the means of.
d.e: I'd know you anywhere by your gravelly voice.

d.t: Indicates an authority according to which something is done.
d.e: By the power vested in me, I now pronounce you man and wife.

d.t: Indicates a means of classification or organisation.
d.e: I sorted the items by category.

d.t: Indicates the amount of change, difference or discrepancy
d.e: Our stock is up by ten percent.

d.t: In the formulae X by X and by Xs, indicates a steady progression, one X after another.
d.e: We went through the book page by page.

d.t: [with the] Acted on in units of the specified size or measure. (Sometimes hyperbolically)
d.e: sold by the yard; cheaper if bought by the gross

d.t: Along a path which runs past someone or something.
d.e: I watched the parade as it passed by.

d.t: In the vicinity, near.
d.e: There was a shepherd close by.

d.t: To or at a place, as a residence or place of business.
d.e: I'll stop by on my way home from work.

d.t: (uncommon outside the phrase 'put by') Aside, away.
d.e: The women spent much time after harvest putting jams by for winter and spring.

d.t: (uncommon except in set phrases) Beyond or past a certain point.
d.e: I'll somehow manage to get by.

d.t: Out of the way, off to one side.
d.e: a by path; a by room

d.t: Subsidiary, incidental.
d.e: by catch; a by issue

d.t: Alternative form of bye.
Dated form of bye (“goodbye”).
(conjunctive, idiomatic) Incidentally; used in referencing a parenthetical statement not timely, central, or crucial to the topic at hand; foregone, passed by, something that has already happened.
d.e: His mother will be coming for dinner tomorrow, and, by the way, she recently sold her collection of ceramic eggs.
